trivia_fact: TCP/IP won over the OSI model not because it was technically superior, but because it was free and already working. The OSI model was still being debated by committee when TCP/IP had a running internet. Vint Cerf later joked that OSI stood for "Oh, So Incomplete."

The "Request for Comments" name was chosen by Steve Crocker in 1969 to sound deliberately informal and non-authoritative — he was a grad student and didn't want to seem presumptuous issuing official standards. The humble name stuck and now governs the entire internet.

Tim Berners-Lee didn't actually choose port 80 — IANA assigned it in 1991 after HTTP was already running on various ports. Before the assignment, early web servers often used port 2784 or 8001. Port 80 was simply the next available number in the range.

Port 443 was assigned to HTTPS in 1994 by Kipp Hickman of Netscape. It was chosen because it was an available port close to 80 — there's no deeper technical reason. The gap between 80 and 443 reflects the hundreds of services registered to ports in between.

Tatu Ylönen, SSH's inventor, chose port 22 deliberately because it sat between telnet (23) and FTP (21) — the two protocols he aimed to replace. He simply emailed IANA requesting it and got the assignment within minutes, as the port was unused.

The ephemeral port range (used for client-side connections) has changed over the decades. BSD originally used 1024-4999, Linux used 32768-61000, and IANA eventually standardized 49152-65535. Many systems still deviate from the standard.

The 1996 SYN flood attack against Panix (a New York ISP) was the first major denial-of-service to weaponize the TCP handshake. It directly led to the invention of SYN cookies by Daniel J. Bernstein — an elegant stateless defense still used today.

There is no IPv5 because version 5 was already assigned to the Internet Stream Protocol (ST), an experimental real-time streaming protocol from 1979 that never gained adoption. When the next-gen IP was designed, it had to skip to version 6.

MAC stands for Media Access Control, but the six-byte format was designed by Xerox for the original Ethernet in 1973. The first three bytes (OUI) identify the manufacturer — you can look up any device's vendor from its MAC address.

Ethernet's 1500-byte MTU was a compromise in the late 1970s. Larger frames meant better throughput but required more buffer memory, which was expensive. 1500 bytes balanced performance against the cost of RAM — about $1000/KB at the time. The value has never changed.

The word "packet" was coined by Donald Davies at the UK National Physical Laboratory in 1965, independently of Paul Baran's "message blocks" at RAND. Davies chose "packet" by analogy with small parcels of mail. The British term won out over Baran's American terminology.

ARP exists because Ethernet predates IP. Ethernet uses MAC addresses, IP uses IP addresses, and neither was designed to know about the other. ARP was a pragmatic hack — a broadcast protocol that asks "who has this IP?" — and it's remained essentially unchanged since 1982.

The first ARPANET routing worked by having each node maintain a table updated via neighbor gossip — the "distance vector" approach. It was so prone to counting-to-infinity loops that it inspired the split-horizon and poison-reverse fixes still used in protocols like RIP today.

Traceroute works by exploiting a side effect of TTL (Time To Live). It sends packets with TTL=1, then 2, then 3, etc. Each router that decrements TTL to zero is required by RFC to send back an ICMP "time exceeded" error — inadvertently revealing its identity. Van Jacobson wrote the original in 1987.

BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is often called "the duct tape of the internet" because the global routing system depends on ~80,000 autonomous systems trusting each other's announcements with minimal verification. A single misconfiguration can (and regularly does) reroute global traffic.

DNS primarily uses UDP because the original designers (Mockapetris, 1983) wanted responses to fit in a single packet for speed. Port 53 was assigned simply as the next available port. DNS falls back to TCP for responses over 512 bytes — a limit that EDNS0 later extended to 4096.

The `ping` command was written by Mike Muuss in 1983 and named after the sound sonar makes. Muuss was explicit that it was not an acronym — backronyms like "Packet InterNet Groper" appeared later and annoyed him. He wrote the entire tool in a single evening.

Bob Metcalfe named Ethernet after "luminiferous ether" — the disproven 19th-century theory of a medium that permeated all space and carried light waves. He chose it because the network cable was the shared passive medium that carried signals to all stations.

The entire 127.0.0.0/8 block (16.7 million addresses) is reserved for loopback — an absurdly large allocation decided in 1981 when address space seemed infinite. Only 127.0.0.1 is commonly used. The "1" was simply the first usable address in the block.

Network Address Translation was designed in 1994 as a short-term workaround while IPv6 was being finalized. Over 30 years later, NAT remains fundamental to internet architecture and has arguably delayed IPv6 adoption by making IPv4 address exhaustion survivable.

Bandwidth originally referred to the width of a frequency band in radio engineering (measured in hertz). Its use for data throughput (bits per second) is technically a misnomer that became universal. Purists still distinguish between bandwidth (capacity) and throughput (actual transfer rate).

The original TCP specification limited the receive window to 64KB because the window field was 16 bits. This made TCP unusably slow on high-latency, high-bandwidth links. RFC 1323 (1992) added window scaling, multiplying the field by powers of 2, enabling windows up to 1GB.

Over 95% of intercontinental internet traffic travels through submarine fiber optic cables, not satellites. These cables are roughly the diameter of a garden hose. Google and other providers now wrap cables in Kevlar-like material partly because sharks were biting through them, possibly attracted by electromagnetic fields.

Wi-Fi doesn't stand for "Wireless Fidelity." The Wi-Fi Alliance hired the brand consultancy Interbrand to create a catchier name than "IEEE 802.11b Direct Sequence." The name was chosen purely for its phonetic similarity to "Hi-Fi." A tagline "The Standard for Wireless Fidelity" was briefly used but later dropped.

Light in fiber optic cable travels at roughly 200,000 km/s (about 2/3 the speed of light in vacuum due to refraction). This means the absolute minimum round-trip latency between New York and London is about 56ms. Real-world latency (~70ms) is remarkably close to this physical limit.
